title: 95% of Vietnamese Want Change: How Local Support Is Reshaping the Dog Trade
excerpt: As Vietnam grapples with rabies outbreaks and pet theft crises, 95% of Vietnamese citizens support ending the dog meat trade. Recent developments in Hanoi show how public backing is driving real policy shifts.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

Vietnam stands at a turning point. While rabies deaths surge among traders and pet theft rings escalate nationwide, the nation's own citizens are leading the charge for change. With 95% public support for ending the trade, recent policy pilots in Hanoi prove that Vietnamese voices—not foreign pressure—are the real engine of transformation.

Key Findings

Hanoi's Voluntary Exit: 4 Traders Close, 18 More Register for Transition

In a landmark shift, four Hanoi-based dog and cat meat traders have voluntarily closed their businesses following livelihood transition workshops run jointly by Hanoi's Department of Livestock, Fisheries and Veterinary Medicine, Soi Dog Foundation, and SBCC Vietnam. More significantly, 18 additional traders have registered to participate in the transition programme, signaling growing momentum. One business owner, Tran Thi Phuong, explained the shift plainly: "When the supply chain lacks adequate traceability or disease control, I understand that both sellers and buyers are facing unnecessary dangers." This is not external pressure rebranded—it's Vietnamese traders recognizing local health threats and making their own economic pivot.

The pilot, approved by Hanoi's government in July 2025, explicitly targets Vietnam's National Target Programme goal of zero rabies deaths by 2030. These closures demonstrate that when Vietnamese traders understand the genuine public health case—and are offered alternative livelihoods—change happens at grassroots level.

Death Without a Bite: Rabies Spreads to Traders, Not Just Handlers

On April 20, 2026, a 58-year-old dog meat trader in Dong Thap province died of rabies without being bitten by an animal. The man had no recorded dog bite but died after weeks of handling uninspected dog meat sourced from unregulated slaughterhouses. His case underscores a critical public health reality: the disease can transmit through minor skin abrasions or contact with infected meat. Dong Thap authorities launched contact-tracing and vaccination protocols immediately, reinforcing that rabies is not a distant threat but a present occupational hazard for traders themselves. This isn't an argument imported from abroad—it's Vietnamese epidemiologists and local health officials sounding the alarm based on real deaths in real Vietnamese communities.

Pet Theft Explodes: Police Dismantle Networks, Rescue Dozens

Meanwhile, organized pet theft continues to fuel underground dog trade networks. On April 18, 2026, Hanoi police arrested two men transporting 10 stolen dogs using homemade stun guns and electrocution devices. In Gia Lai province, authorities dismantled a major theft ring responsible for stealing approximately 5,200 dogs—52 tonnes—generating roughly 2.6 billion Vietnamese đồng in illegal proceeds. Critically, these enforcement actions reflect Vietnam's own police and enforcement priorities: protecting Vietnamese families' pets and securing Vietnamese neighborhoods. The public supports these operations because the theft crisis is hitting Vietnamese households directly. This local ownership of the issue—protecting family pets, not imposing foreign values—is the bedrock of sustainable change.

From Trade to Transition: Hanoi's Model Shows Economic Viability of Change

Hanoi's transitional pilot program explicitly combines rabies prevention with livelihood support for traders, addressing the economic argument head-on. Rather than shutting businesses overnight, the city government offers retraining and alternative income streams. The fact that 22 traders (4 closed + 18 registered) have engaged voluntarily—without a total ban in place—demonstrates that Vietnamese businesses recognize both the health imperative and the economic pathway forward. This bottom-up, consent-based approach aligns perfectly with the 95% Vietnamese public support for ending the trade: citizens want change, traders are responding, and government is facilitating the transition. No imported mandate; just Vietnamese solving a Vietnamese problem.

Also Worth Noting

  • Ho Chi Minh City Rabies Deaths Surge — Three confirmed rabies deaths by April 20, 2026, exceed the entire 2025 total for the city, with summer heat expected to intensify transmission risk.
  • Coordinated Pet Theft Rings Operate Nationwide — Large-scale networks using specialized equipment operate across northern provinces, targeting family pets specifically for meat market sale.
  • Hanoi's Enforcement Tightens Simultaneously — While transition programs operate, city authorities are also increasing inspections, traceability requirements, and licensing controls on remaining vendors.
  • Rabies Clusters Detected in Multiple Provinces — At least 42 animal disease outbreaks across 26 communes in 9 provinces signal widespread circulation linked to uncontrolled dog slaughter and transport.
